title: How do you make your game not run like crap?
author: Such--Balance
selftext:
I lack coding experience. Obviously. Just been piling up more and more mechanisms and effects on top of each other.

Im making an in essence, pretty simple 2d tower defense game. But have lots of added shaders, automatic territory expansion, enemy pathfinding, lights and shadows etc etc.

Im sure the architacture absolutely sucks as im nearing the limit of playable fps. And i havent even made anything remotely how i want it to end up.

Any basic tips or tricks to clean or polish this with ai?

Any fuctional prompts to introduce massive ups savings? A few things i got planned myself is to cull a lot of effects based on zoom level and obv location of camera.

In general, is optimizing games just a matter of loads of small incremental gains or do i just need to chalk it up as a nice first try and move to a never project with a clearer architecture from the ground up?

comments.author: BroadswordGames
comments.body:
Ask your client to create a comprehensive plan to optimize your game for performance and build file size using it's understanding of the code base and techniques found online without breaking any of the existing functionality, textures, animations or anything that a player would notice.

Then run the plan efficiently with multiple agents

comments.author: Livid_Shallot5701
comments.body:
the first thing i did with a new game idea is: tell opus how the endgoal is, like how many figures run around thinking, having needs, fighting, working, pathfinding, and how many buildings  i wanna support in the most crowded places like a parade of the whole army in the main city etc. and i let it make a testsuit for the engines with some random assets with the correct poligon count, let it make stresstests and add a lot of random cpu and gpu calculation on top of that on sliders, so we can stresstest the maximum and then let it plan out the game architecture from there. 

and then i build a core document, where it always referrs to "hoch much action systems will get" and let it strictly plan everything as little as possible. i had opus 5.5 tell me "ah, so its only 0,7ms so its not a problem" and i told it "yeah but 400 people doing it is still no problem? and if we add 100 of those systems, each costing "only" 0,7ms is it still not a problem? and it immediately shuts up and writes some dll so it goes down by like 1/100th or 1/1000th of cost. 

and i do that for every new mechanic and be very strict, some flowers only costing 0,007ms i will still ask it if its optimized or if it can divide that by 10 etc.

comments.author: Designer-Camp1815
comments.body: I set a performance target early (95% of frames faster than 7ms) and Claude is generally aware of it when working. When adding a new visual effect I have Claude estimate the performance impact to get an idea if we need to design conservatively. To test there is a benchmark that has a loop of real, repeatable gameplay with a whole bunch of profiling attached. Claude can then run multiple passes of this to remove noise and work out why specific frames are slow. Claude proposes an optimization, makes it then does a benchmark to see if it actually helped. It doesn't always work.

comments.author: 0bscuris
comments.body:
I think this is the toughest part for people without a background in code because ai will write the script like, every frame check everything and then the system is dragging but in reality, you don’t need to check everything and u can’t read the code to see what it is doing. 

So if ur characters r asking, am i the right sprite and shader? Every frame, or saying where do i move next? Every frame instead of generating a list of points to move to and spot checking/changing that list when something happens. 

For example: you don’t need a new path everytime if nothing has changed. if ur placing buildings or something, you place a building at a location and it can shoot x distance, then only the pre existing paths that pass through that new information need to be recaculated, enemies on otherside of the map don’t care and can just keep using the path list they have. 

If can break the map into essentially sectors, lets say for example you place something in west sector, ok, now you can tell it, check only the enemies on the west sector list to recalc pathfinding, everyone else just keep looping through the coordinate list. 

What causes drag on modern hardware is checking tons of game objects, tons of times. 

Same with sprites, asking am i dead? Every frame is expensive. Asking, “i have just been shot, am i dead?” Is much cheaper cuz the script is only running when something happens

comments.author: do-sieg

If you use shaders for things that could be done in another way (animated sprite), take screenshots of the animation, make a sprite sheet and drop the shader.
If you have full screen effects, make sure they only run when needed.

And yeah, just ask Opus to run an audit and you may reduce half your issues with one or two simple updates.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
Most performance is about either intelligent caching or running intelligent searches or both of those things, minimizing asset loading on the spot and/or redundant cycles.

If you see a performance issue in the game, ask Opus or Astra about it; they'll usually suggest a cache based solution or a way to make a search algorithm more efficient.

There's actually quite a lot you can learn about the fundamentals of efficiency in coding (and the trade-offs from it) by comparing normal delay-based netcode to rollback netcode. Even for just my little single-player game projects, the base principle is that it is better for your game to make a solid, educated guess about what to do next rather than try to anticipate every possibility and wait for answers to every query.

We anticipate the edge cases and plan for them, but we do not wait to consider every edge case before the game goes to the next frame. We make an assumption, and we go to the next frame. 95% of the time, the assumption is right. 99.99999\~% of the time, either the assumption is right OR the assumption is wrong in a way that can be corrected for between frames when the anticipated edge case is encountered, so the player literally never notices that the game has corrected a mistake.

And what about that tiny fraction of a fraction of a fraction of a percent of the time that the game needs to visually correct a mistake it has already rendered?

Nobody cares. It looks smooth, and the player's brain literally tricks them into not seeing the mistake as a result.

The undo is less noticeable than the delay.

Your game should run code like you should run a date - confidently guess and assume the best; apologize later if needed.

comments.author: je386
comments.body:
Make sure that expensive tasks (that need much computing power or memory) are not inside of loops, if possible. You can save much performance by precomputing values instead of computing everything on the fly.

I had this with tiles. A map of just 40x40 tiles amounts to 1600 tiles and if something is done for each tile, the function runs 1600 times. You can check if this can be precomputed, if you can except many tiles or only do the function for visible tiles.

comments.author: Mikeality
comments.body:
I'm fairly new to AI programming, but have been programming for nearly 15 years now, so take this with a grain of salt.

I believe that even as AI gets better and better at coding, the humans involved are going to still need to have their coding ability be good. When working on a project where the final product is the goal, AI should do most if not all coding. However, you should still work on some training projects where you do the coding yourself for the sake of learning the trade. Either entirely independent of AI, or having it on the side in more of an advisory role to explain things. It's like football players lifting weights. Nobody is lifting weights on the field. But the players who do come out stronger in a way that directly improves their performance.

The reality is that there are no easy or simple tricks that will save you a lot of performance. A poorly running program where you're not familiar with the code itself is like a tangled up rope you just pulled tightly into a knot. The whole thing needs to be carefully untangled, and the best approach would have been to carefully build it up in the first place without getting tangled. Whether you're fixing it or building it right the first time, you just need coding knowledge and experience to do it.

That being said, there may be some things you can do on the meantime. This strategy will still apply even as you become a good coder, it's been my approach so far and is working fairly well. You have to always take time and have the AI draft a plan before letting it work. Give feedback and iterate on the drafts. Once you have a solid plan, it needs to be broken up into working parts. Stages of development where you isolate the building blocks of features as finely as possible. Each of these isolated blocks then needs to have clear tests defined. Tests should focus on a variety of aspects. It needs to logically accomplish its goal, and another would be it needs to do so within a clearly defined performance constraint. 

Right now, AI is not quite smart enough to just tell it "make my entire program run in less than half a second." This might work for simple programs, but not games. What can work, is if you isolate something like "make the enemy pathfinding calculation run within 200ms" you can iterate on that feature until it's working and working within the performance constraints. At that point, you can finalize that feature, log it into git, and move on to the next one. If done right, all the building blocks will be within range and your final program will be too.

comments.author: FrozenFirebat
comments.body: you gave us very little to go on. what are you developing this game on? threejs, godot, unity, unreal? Do you have an agent run nightly that measures your profiler on a quiet machine? Are you sure that you're frustum culling? you have a lot of shaders? are they loading lazily or are they preloaded before level loaded? same with your other assets? is everything single threaded? are your shaders compiled JIT?
